s1_definition.profdef: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` provides TWO locks: a **readLock** (shared — multiple readers simultaneously) and a **writeLock** (exclusive — blocks all readers and other writers). When reads vastly outnumber writes (90%+ reads), it IMPROVES performance: 100 readers run in PARALLEL instead of sequential. When writes are FREQUENT, it HURTS: every write blocks ALL readers, and the overhead of maintaining reader counts (CAS on shared counter) costs more than a simple `ReentrantLock`. Properties: reentrant (same thread can lock multiple times), optional fairness (FIFO ordering), write lock can downgrade to read lock (but NOT upgrade).
s1_definition.analogy: **ReentrantLock** = one person at a time in the vault, whether reading or writing. 100 people checking balances? ONE at a time! **ReadWriteLock** = multiple people can READ the register simultaneously (readLock). But when someone WRITES (writeLock), everyone else leaves until the write is done. Read-heavy (90% reads): 100 readers simultaneously → 100x throughput! Write-heavy (50% writes): constant lock switching → overhead → slower than simple lock.
s1_definition.oneliner: ReadWriteLock: many concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. Read-heavy = big win (parallel reads). Write-heavy = overhead (reader count CAS + write blocks all). Use when reads >> writes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `ReentrantReadWriteLock` provides TWO locks: a **readLock** (shared — multiple readers simultaneously) and a **writeLock** (exclusive — blocks all readers and other writers). When reads vastly outnumber writes (90%+ reads), it IMPROVES performance: 100 readers run in PARALLEL instead of sequential. When writes are FREQUENT, it HURTS: every write blocks ALL readers, and the overhead of maintaining reader counts (CAS on shared counter) costs more than a simple `ReentrantLock`. Properties: reentrant (same thread can lock multiple times), optional fairness (FIFO ordering), write lock can downgrade to read lock (but NOT upgrade).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **ReentrantLock** = one person at a time in the vault, whether reading or writing. 100 people checking balances? ONE at a time! **ReadWriteLock** = multiple people can READ the register simultaneously (readLock). But when someone WRITES (writeLock), everyone else leaves until the write is done. Read-heavy (90% reads): 100 readers simultaneously → 100x throughput! Write-heavy (50% writes): constant lock switching → overhead → slower than simple lock.

**One line to remember:** ReadWriteLock: many concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. Read-heavy = big win (parallel reads). Write-heavy = overhead (reader count CAS + write blocks all). Use when reads >> writes.

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The account balance cache served 10K reads/sec and 50 writes/sec.** With `ReentrantLock`: all 10K reads sequential — each waited for the lock. P99: 5ms. Fix: `ReentrantReadWriteLock` — 10K readers run in PARALLEL (readLock shared), 50 writers exclusive. P99: 0.2ms. 25x improvement. BUT: when they also cached trade history (500 writes/sec, 500 reads/sec — 50:50), ReadWriteLock was SLOWER than ReentrantLock due to reader-count CAS contention. Used plain ReentrantLock for that cache.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** 10 reader threads call `readLock().lock()` → ALL 10 acquire simultaneously (shared!). `getReadLockCount() = 10`.

**Step 2.** Writer calls `writeLock().lock()` → waits until all 10 readers release → acquires exclusively → updates balance → releases.

**Step 3.** Readers resume → all see updated balance (happens-before via lock/unlock).
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ ReadWriteLock ═══

  READ-HEAVY (95% reads):
  Reader-1: readLock() ✅ ─┐
  Reader-2: readLock() ✅ ─┤── ALL concurrent! Parallel!
  Reader-N: readLock() ✅ ─┘
  Writer:   writeLock() → WAITS until all readers release → exclusive!

  WRITE-HEAVY (50% writes):
  Reader: readLock() → CAS on readerCount → contention!
  Writer: writeLock() → blocks all readers → frequent blocking!
  Overhead > benefit → use plain ReentrantLock instead!

  ═══ DECISION ═══
  reads >> writes (95:5): ReadWriteLock ✅ (parallel reads!)
  reads ≈ writes (50:50): ReentrantLock ✅ (less overhead)
  reads >>> writes (99.9:0.1): StampedLock ✅ (optimistic, zero CAS!)
```

```
  ═══ HLD — Lock Selection for Balance Cache ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Balance Cache Service                             │

  │  10K reads/sec, 50 writes/sec (99.5:0.5):        │

```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — ReentrantReadWriteLock ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReentrantReadWriteLock               │
  │  - sync: AQS (state = readers|writer)│
  │  - state high 16 bits: reader count  │
  │  - state low 16 bits: writer count   │
  │  + readLock(): ReadLock              │  shared (CAS on reader count)
  │  + writeLock(): WriteLock            │  exclusive
  │  + isFair(): boolean                 │
  │  + getReadLockCount(): int           │
  │  + isWriteLocked(): boolean          │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ReadLock.lock():  CAS: state += (1 << 16)  → reader count++
  WriteLock.lock(): CAS: state = 1            → exclusive (waits for 0 readers)
  
  Downgrade: hold write → acquire read → release write → now read-only!
  Upgrade:   hold read → acquire write → DEADLOCK! (can't upgrade!)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
ReentrantReadWriteLock provides a shared readLock (multiple concurrent readers) and an exclusive writeLock (blocks all readers and writers). It IMPROVES performance when reads vastly outnumber writes (95%+ reads): 100 readers run in parallel instead of sequential — massive throughput gain. It HURTS when writes are frequent (50:50): every readLock requires a CAS on the shared reader count (contention), and frequent writes block all readers — more overhead than a simple ReentrantLock.

Decision guide: 99:1 read:write → StampedLock optimistic (zero CAS reads). 95:5 → ReadWriteLock (parallel reads, occasional write blocking). 50:50 → ReentrantLock (simplest, least overhead). Properties: reentrant, optional fairness (FIFO), write-to-read downgrade (allowed), read-to-write upgrade (NOT allowed — deadlock). In banking: balance cache (10K reads/sec, 50 writes/sec) → ReadWriteLock: P99 0.2ms (25x better than ReentrantLock's 5ms). Trade history (50:50) → ReentrantLock (simpler, faster for balanced workload).
